body:
Global crypto markets ripped higher on August 20, with total market capitalization climbing to $2.39T, a gain of 5.11% in 24 hours, on volume of $127.8B. The Fear & Greed Index swung from 46 yesterday to 62 today, a single-session move from Fear to Greed that captures the speed and conviction of the reversal. Bearish positioning was obliterated in the process: per CoinDesk reporting, short sellers lost a record $2.7B as bitcoin surged toward $70,000, and one notable trader who had made $49M shorting crypto lost $24M on ether alone in 12 seconds. That is not a market drifting higher on thin volume — that is a short squeeze layered on top of genuine institutional inflow.

BTC printed $69,531 at time of writing, up 8.80% over 24 hours and 9.40% over 7 days, on volume of $51.95B. The asset briefly touched $70,000 intraday, the first time that level was reclaimed since June, before pulling back slightly. The $70,000 figure now becomes the most important near-term level on the chart: a clean hold above it would open the door to the prior all-time high range, while failure to recapture it on a closing basis would likely hand the initiative back to sellers who survived the squeeze. BTC dominance sits at 58.3%, which is still elevated but worth watching if altcoin momentum continues to accelerate — any meaningful dominance compression from here would signal a rotation trade rather than a pure BTC story.

ETH was the standout single-name move today, up 18.50% to $2,247.04 on volume of $32.01B, decisively outpacing bitcoin and dragging ETH dominance to 11.3%. CoinDesk noted inflows of $189M into ether ETF products, alongside $517M into bitcoin ETFs, in what they described as the biggest combined inflows in months — that institutional demand channel is clearly open and functioning. SOL added 11.90% to $86.0 on $5.04B in volume, and XRP gained 11.20% to $1.11 on $3.24B in volume, putting both firmly in the top performers alongside ETH. LINK quietly posted a 10.10% 24-hour gain and a 20.40% 7-day gain to $10.53, a divergence from its relatively low volume of $0.72B that suggests this is genuine price discovery rather than a wash-trade pop. On the lagging end, ADA managed only +5.30% to $0.1838, DOT only +4.70% to $0.7866, and BNB +4.80% to $628.43 — all still positive, but the gap between these and the leaders is wide enough to constitute a meaningful divergence worth monitoring. HYPE jumped 20%, per Cointelegraph, after Trump signaled legal US regulatory clarity for Hyperliquid.

The macro catalyst set here is unusually dense for a single session. On the regulatory front, Trump is publicly pushing for passage of the CLARITY Act alongside crypto industry leaders, but Congressman Gallego warned that a rushed vote could actually set the legislation back — a tension that makes the near-term legislative path genuinely uncertain. The UAE stablecoin integration news is incremental but consistent with the broader trend of dollar-denominated digital settlement rails expanding into non-US jurisdictions. Underlying all of this is a market that read the ETF inflow data — $517M into BTC products, $189M into ETH products — as a decisive signal that institutional allocation is re-accelerating, and priced accordingly in a matter of hours.

The next 48 hours are high-stakes. Whether BTC can close convincingly above $70,000 is the single most important technical question, because a failure there will be cited immediately as a double-top signal and could reverse much of today's move. On the ETH side, watch whether the 18.50% day attracts follow-through buying or triggers profit-taking from players who bought the lows — the $2,247 level is not a historically significant resistance zone, but the speed of the move leaves air underneath. Legislative noise around the CLARITY Act will also matter: any credible signal of either acceleration or delay will move the regulatory-sensitive names. The short-squeeze washout of $2.7B in bearish bets removes a key structural tailwind for further upside velocity, so the next leg higher, if it comes, will need to be driven by fresh demand rather than forced covering.
